title: SSH Brute Force and Unauthorized Access Investigation Runbook
source: NIST SP 800-123 (Guide to General Server Security) & MITRE ATT&CK T1110
content:
### 1. OVERVIEW & DETECTION
SSH brute force attacks involve automated repeated attempts to guess credentials for SSH services (port 22). Threat actors employ dictionary attacks, password spraying, or credential stuffing across common administrative usernames (e.g., root, admin, ubuntu, test, oracle). Detection indicators include:
- High volume of failed authentication events in short intervals from single or distributed source IP addresses.
- Failed password or invalid user log messages in authentication logs.
- Anomalous successful authentication immediately following dozens or hundreds of failed login attempts.
- Unexpected geographic origin or off-hours SSH sessions for critical infrastructure servers.

### 2. EVIDENCE & ARTIFACTS TO EXAMINE
- Linux Authentication Logs: /var/log/auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL/CentOS) searching for strings such as Failed password for invalid user, Accepted publickey, Accepted password, and Connection closed by authenticating user.
- Journalctl System Logs: journalctl -u ssh or journalctl -u sshd examining timestamp spikes and IP addresses.
- Current Active Sessions: Run who, w, last, and lastb (failed login records) to identify active SSH sessions and user history.
- SSH Configuration: /etc/ssh/sshd_config checking PermitRootLogin, PasswordAuthentication, and AllowUsers settings.
- User Authorized Keys: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys across all system accounts to detect unauthorized public keys added by attackers.

### 3. INVESTIGATION & TRIAGE
- Determine Outcome: Verify whether the brute force attempts succeeded. If an Accepted log entry exists following a series of Failed entries from the same IP, treat the alert as a verified host compromise.
- Post-Authentication Activity: If an unauthorized login occurred, examine bash history (~/.bash_history), executed binaries, cron jobs (/etc/cron*, /var/spool/cron/), and network listeners (ss -tulpn or netstat -tulpn).
- Threat Intelligence IP Check: Check source IP addresses against threat intelligence feeds to differentiate broad internet background noise from targeted campaign infrastructure.

### 4. CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES
- Immediate IP Block: Add malicious source IP addresses or subnets to firewall rules via iptables, nftables, ufw, or cloud security groups (e.g., iptables -A INPUT -s <Attacker_IP> -j DROP).
- Terminate Unauthorized Sessions: Kill active rogue sessions using pkill -KILL -u <Compromised_User> or kill -9 <PID>.
- Account Suspension & Key Revocation: Lock compromised user accounts (passwd -l <Username>) and remove untrusted SSH public keys from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

### 5. ERADICATION, RECOVERY & REMEDIATION
- Disable Password Authentication: Enforce public key authentication by setting PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.
- Disable Root Login: Configure PermitRootLogin no to prevent direct administrative brute force.
- Deploy Fail2ban / CrowdSec: Implement automated rate-limiting daemons that dynamically block source IPs exceeding failed attempt thresholds.
- Network Boundary Restrictions: Restrict SSH port access to corporate VPNs, bastion jump hosts, or management CIDR blocks rather than exposing port 22 directly to the public internet.
